scenarios.d: Something was taken, kept, obtained by deception, damaged or forged.

qs.q: Was property or money taken, kept or obtained from someone?
Was it movable property — cash, phone, vehicle, goods?
qs.h: Land and buildings are immovable; taking them is usually a civil matter.

qs.q: Was it taken without the owner's consent?
Did the person intend to keep it or use it dishonestly?
Was it seized suddenly or forcibly from the person — a chain, a bag, a phone?
Was force used, or fear of immediate hurt caused, at the time of taking?
Were five or more people involved together?
Was the property handed over because of a threat of future harm?
Had the property been entrusted to the person — for safekeeping, carriage, or as an employee or agent?
Was the owner deceived by false facts or a false promise, and handed over property because of it?
Did someone enter a building, premises or vehicle intending to commit an offence?
Was a document, signature or electronic record forged or altered?
Was property destroyed or damaged?

rules.why: Movable property was taken out of another's possession without consent, with a dishonest intention.
The taking was sudden or forcible from the person — the additional element that makes it snatching.
Force, or the fear of immediate hurt, was used in order to take the property — robbery rather than theft.
Robbery committed by five or more persons together is dacoity.
Property was delivered because of a threat of injury — extortion, even if no force was used at the time.
Property that had been entrusted was misappropriated — criminal breach of trust rather than theft.
Property belonging to another was dishonestly converted to the person's own use.
A deception induced the delivery of property — cheating.
Entry into property in another's possession with intent to commit an offence is criminal trespass.
A false document or electronic record was made — forgery.
Property was destroyed or its value diminished — mischief.

scenarios.d: Force was used against a person, and someone was hurt, threatened or killed.

qs.q: Was physical force used against a person?
Was anyone injured?
Was the injury serious — a fracture, permanent loss of sight or hearing, or an injury endangering life?
qs.h: Section 117 lists the eight categories of grievous hurt.

qs.q: Was a weapon or other dangerous means used?
Did anyone die?
Was there an intention to cause death, or knowledge that death was likely?
Was the act rash or negligent rather than deliberate?
Did the act fall short — an attempt rather than a completed act?
Was anyone threatened with injury to person, reputation or property?
Was the person acting to defend themselves or another from an attack?

rules.why: Death was caused with the intention of causing death, or with knowledge that it was likely — murder, punishable under s. 103.
Death was caused without the intention or knowledge that makes it murder — culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
Death was caused by a rash or negligent act rather than a deliberate one.
The act fell short of death but was done with the intention or knowledge required for murder — attempt to murder.
The injury caused falls within the categories of grievous hurt.
Grievous hurt was caused by a dangerous weapon or means — the aggravated form.
Bodily pain, disease or infirmity was caused — hurt.
Hurt was caused with an instrument for shooting, stabbing or cutting, or other dangerous means.
A threat of injury was made with intent to cause alarm or to compel an act — criminal intimidation.
Force used in private defence is not an offence at all — see ss. 34 to 44 for the limits.
An attempt to commit an offence is itself punishable under the general attempt provision.

scenarios.d: Conduct towards a woman or a child — harassment, force, marriage-related cruelty or trafficking.

qs.q: Was the person affected a woman?
Was there unwanted physical contact, or a demand or request for sexual favours?
Were sexually coloured remarks made, or pornography shown?
Was she followed, or contacted against her wishes, or watched online?
Were images taken or watched of her in a private act?
Was she assaulted or subjected to criminal force intending to outrage her modesty or to disrobe her?
Was there sexual intercourse without consent?
Was she subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relatives?
Was the cruelty or harassment in connection with a demand for dowry?
Did she die within seven years of marriage, by burns or bodily injury, in circumstances that were not natural?
Was a child under eighteen involved?

rules.why: Intercourse took place without consent, falling within the definition in s. 63. Punishment is under s. 64.
Assault or criminal force was used on a woman with intent to outrage her modesty.
Unwelcome physical contact or a demand for sexual favours is sexual harassment under s. 75.
Sexually coloured remarks or showing pornography fall within the fourth clause of s. 75.
Watching or capturing images of a woman in a private act without consent is voyeurism.
Following or contacting a woman against her wishes, or monitoring her online, is stalking.
Death within seven years of marriage following dowry-related cruelty — dowry death.
Cruelty by the husband or a relative of the husband, as defined in the explanation to s. 85.
Taking a child out of lawful guardianship is kidnapping — see also s. 137(2) for punishment.
Recruiting, transporting or harbouring a child for exploitation is trafficking under s. 143.

scenarios.d: Group conduct, threats to public peace, or acts against the security of India.

qs.q: Were five or more people assembled with a common object?
Was force or violence used by that group?
Did the words or acts promote enmity or disharmony between groups?
Was this a continuing criminal enterprise run by a group?
Was the act intended to strike terror, or to threaten the sovereignty or security of India?
Did it incite secession or armed rebellion?

rules.why: Force or violence was used by an unlawful assembly — rioting.
An assembly of five or more with a common unlawful object is an unlawful assembly.
Words or acts promoting disharmony or enmity between groups on protected grounds.
Continuing unlawful activity by a crime syndicate is organised crime — a new offence in the Sanhita.
An act intended to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty or security of India is a terrorist act.
Exciting or attempting to excite secession or armed rebellion falls under s. 152, which replaced sedition.

scenarios.d: A collision, a rash act, or a driver who left the scene.

qs.q: Was a motor vehicle involved?
Did anyone die?
Was anyone injured?
Did the driver leave the scene without reporting to the police?
Was the driving rash or negligent, rather than deliberate?

rules.why: Death by rash or negligent driving followed by flight from the scene — s. 106(2), which carries up to ten years.
Death caused by a rash or negligent act — s. 106(1), up to five years.
Injury caused by a rash or negligent act may be charged as hurt; the procedure code and the Motor Vehicles Act also apply.
